title: CERN Begins Dismantling the Large Hadron Collider for a Major Upgrade
summary:
The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) — a 27-kilometer ring of superconducting magnets buried beneath the border of France and Switzerland — is being taken apart. Not to be retired, but to be rebuilt stronger.

On September 7, 2026, CERN teams began dismantling sections of the collider on either side of the ATLAS and CMS experiments. The goal is to remove 28 superconducting magnets, including the crucial "inner triplets" — groups of three quadrupole magnets that focus particle beams as tightly as possible just before collisions. The tighter the beams are compressed, the more collisions occur, which increases the LHC's luminosity.

The replacement is part of the High-Luminosity LHC (HiLumi LHC) project. The new inner triplets use niobium-tin superconducting coils instead of niobium-titanium, allowing them to generate magnetic fields of 11.3 tesla — about 40% stronger than the current magnets. That means more collisions, more data, and more chances to discover new physics.

"The replacement of these magnets with the new HiLumi LHC inner triplets is crucial for the coming high-luminosity years," explains Jean-Philippe Tock, Head of the LS3 Coordination Team. "The first quadrupole of the new triplets should arrive in the tunnel at the start of 2029. In total, 16 cryostats and 28 cryo-assemblies will be installed — a major undertaking."

The current inner triplets date back to the LHC's construction and were installed between 2005 and 2007. After nearly twenty years of operation, they are being retired. "It's truly remarkable to witness such a handover from one generation of innovation to the next," says Markus Zerlauth, the HiLumi LHC Project Leader.

ALICE and LHCb, the other two main experiments, don't need the same increase in instantaneous luminosity, so their existing inner triplets will remain in place — though they will still be upgraded to benefit from the overall luminosity increase.

The work is happening during the third long shutdown (LS3). CERN Director-General Mark Thomson visited LHC Point 1 to mark the milestone. When the LHC restarts, it will be more powerful than ever.
why_it_matters: Fundamental physics advances on the timescale of decades, and decisions about which machines to build and upgrade now shape what scientists can even ask in the 2030s and beyond. This rebuild is also a case study in how enormous, shared international facilities replace their own hardware generation by generation.

background_read: CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research, is an international laboratory near Geneva on the French–Swiss border, funded by more than twenty member states. It built the LHC, the world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator.

The LHC's best-known achievement was the 2012 discovery of the Higgs boson — the particle linked to why other particles have mass — found using the huge ATLAS and CMS detectors positioned around the ring.

Huge accelerators are upgraded in generations. The LHC has had long maintenance periods called 'long shutdowns', and LS3 is the third of these, which allows magnets installed back during the machine's construction in 2005–2007 to be replaced.
Luminosity is the number physicists care about most: it counts how many collisions happen per second, so raising it means more chances to catch rare particles and rare processes.

Superconducting magnets only work when cooled with liquid helium to temperatures colder than outer space, which is why the machine depends on enormous cryogenic plants and on components such as cryostats.

perspectives.description: More luminosity means more collisions, so extremely rare events that were invisible before might finally appear. Upgrading a machine that already works is far cheaper and faster than building a brand-new collider from scratch.

The shutdown and upgrade absorb enormous funding and years of machine time, with no guarantee that higher luminosity reveals anything beyond the current model of particle physics. Long shutdowns also disrupt younger researchers, who depend on fresh data to publish.

Large accelerators are upgraded in generations — new magnets, new cryogenics, new detectors — each designed to push past the limits of the last. Replacing hardware installed in the mid-2000s is ordinary engineering as much as it is frontier research.

perspectives.perspective: The road to the next machine
perspectives.description: The first new quadrupole should arrive in the tunnel around 2029, after which the LHC is expected to run for many years with far more collisions. Meanwhile, CERN and other laboratories are already debating what kind of collider should come after it.
